power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: What is already known on this topic?
Neisseria gonorrhoeae diagnostic escape mutants for the Xpert® CT/NG assay (Cepheid), lacking one or both diagnostic targets, have recently been identified in England and internationally.
However, the true prevalence of these mutants and their impact on diagnoses are unknown.

What this study adds Whilst 99.7% of specimens were confirmed as gonorrhoeanegative, this study identified two confirmed and one suspected diagnostic escape mutants among 978 Xpert® NG-negative specimens, from two sexual health services.

These findings demonstrate that Xpert® NG escape mutants are present in clinic attendees in England, and may result in missed gonorrhoea diagnoses How this study might affect research, practice or policy The findings from this study support surveillance for diagnostic escape mutants and further studies to establish their prevalence and clinical impact.
NOTE: This preprint reports new research that has not been certified by peer review and should not be used to guide clinical practice.

Gonorrhoea, caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae (NG), is the second most common sexually transmitted bacterial infection in England with 63,943 diagnoses reported in 2025, 57.6% of which were in gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men (GBMSM) (1).
text.formatted: Gonorrhoea, caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae (NG), is the second most common sexually transmitted bacterial infection in England with 63,943 diagnoses reported in 2025, 57.6% of which were in gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men (GBMSM) <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(1)</ref>.

text.text: Nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) offer superior sensitivity for diagnosis of infection to other methods, such as in vitro culture, particularly for extragenital (2-6) and asymptomatic infections (4, 6, 7).
text.formatted: Nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) offer superior sensitivity for diagnosis of infection to other methods, such as in vitro culture, particularly for extragenital (2-6) and asymptomatic infections <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, NAAT testing can use non-invasive, self-collected samples.

Due to the potential for cross-reactivity of NAATs with commensal Neisseria species, especially in the pharynx, confirmation of positive results is recommended (2) using either a second target within an assay or a separate assay with a different target.
The Xpert® CT/NG assay (Cepheid) is a rapid (<2 h), modular cartridge-based NAAT that detects both Chlamydia trachomatis and NG DNA in one cartridge (4).
text.formatted: The Xpert® CT/NG assay (Cepheid) is a rapid (<2 h), modular cartridge-based NAAT that detects both Chlamydia trachomatis and NG DNA in one cartridge <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(4)</ref>.

text.text: The assay is frequently used as a confirmatory test as part of a two-step NG NAAT algorithm.

The NG component of the assay has two chromosomal gonorrhoeaspecific targets: NG2 and NG4, approximately 4 Kb apart, and amplification in both is required for the GeneXpert® (Cepheid) software to report a positive result.

In June 2025, the national STI Reference Laboratory (STIRL) at the UK Health Security Agency confirmed the identification of a NG diagnostic escape mutant for the Xpert® CT/NG assay, following a likely recombination event with Neisseria meningitidis (8).
text.formatted: In June 2025, the national STI Reference Laboratory (STIRL) at the UK Health Security Agency confirmed the identification of a NG diagnostic escape mutant for the Xpert® CT/NG assay, following a likely recombination event with Neisseria meningitidis <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(8)</ref>.

text.text: Whole-genome sequencing revealed a complete absence of the NG2 and NG4 targets.
A small number (n=16) of further mutants lacking one or both of the Xpert® NG targets were subsequently identified globally (8, 9).
text.formatted: A small number (n=16) of further mutants lacking one or both of the Xpert® NG targets were subsequently identified globally <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9)</ref>.

text.text: Due to the GeneXpert® software algorithm, single target mutants would also be reported as NG negative.
Further analysis of these isolates indicated that recombination events had occurred in multiple distinct genomic lineages and was not the result of clonal spread (8, 9).
text.formatted: Further analysis of these isolates indicated that recombination events had occurred in multiple distinct genomic lineages and was not the result of clonal spread <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9)</ref>.

text.text: The true extent of use of the Cepheid GeneXpert® in England is unknown, however approximately 39.5% of participants of the UK NEQAS C. trachomatis & N. gonorrhoeae external quality assurance scheme reported use of this platform in 2026.
text.formatted: The true extent of use of the Cepheid GeneXpert® in England is unknown, however approximately 39.5% of participants of the UK NEQAS C. trachomatis & N. gonorrhoeae external quality assurance scheme reported use of this platform in 2026.

text.text: Some sexual health services (SHSs), such as those delivered by the Chelsea and Westminster NHS Foundation Trust in London, offer in-clinic testing with the Xpert® CT/NG assay.
These SHSs serve a substantial proportion of SHS attendees nationally and reported 13.4% of the total NG diagnoses from England in 2025 (8,556/63,943) (10).

We undertook an anonymised prospective case finding study of Xpert® NG-negative specimens from individuals attending two Chelsea and Westminster NHS Foundation Trust SHSs, to estimate the prevalence of these diagnostic escape mutants.

Assuming the prevalence of Xpert® NG diagnostic escape mutants was ≤0.3%, it was calculated that at least 998 NG-negative specimens would need to be tested to detect at least one mutant with 95% confidence.
Owing to differences in testing numbers, sampling periods were tailored to each SHS.
Clinic 1 which performed an average of 3,842 NG tests per month in 2025, collected samples during the first week of December 2025 only.
Clinic 2 which averaged 959 NG tests per month, collected samples throughout December 2025.
To ensure representation of different specimen types, only one sample type (e.g. vaginal swab) was selected per day at Clinic 1 and per week at Clinic 2.
Both clinics provide services to individuals of all sexes, gender identities and sexual orientations.
However, Clinic 1 serves a higher proportion of GBMSM.
Residual Xpert® NG-negative specimens (urine, genital or rectal swabs) in Xpert® CT/NG sample collection buffer (Cepheid), were forwarded to STIRL.
Pharyngeal swabs were excluded due to known cross-reactivity of diagnostic assays with commensal Neisseria at this site.
Samples from individuals attending for test-of-cure were also excluded.
Specimens were anonymised (retaining sample site and age), aliquoted and DNA extracted using the QIASymphony and DSP Virus/Pathogen Midi kit (Qiagen).
Extracts were tested using the GeneProof TM Neisseria gonorrhoeae PCR kit (GeneProof) on the QuantStudio 5 (Applied Biosystems), as per manufacturer's instructions.
The assay targets both the NG porA pseudogene and 16S rRNA gene, reporting in the same channel to provide increased sensitivity of detection in specimens with low DNA load.
GeneProof TM NG-positive specimens were retested following re-extraction where possible, or on the original extract if insufficient volume remained.
The limit of detection of the GeneProof TM assay was established locally as 30 colony forming units/mL, equating to a cycle threshold (Ct) value of 37.
As such results were interpreted as follows:

To estimate the potential number of gonorrhoea infections that may have been missed in 2025 due to Xpert® NG escape mutants, the prevalence of confirmed and suspected mutants identified in this study was applied to the total number of NG tests performed at the participating SHSs.
Suspected mutants were GeneProof TMpositive samples that could not undergo repeat testing with the Xpert® CT/NG assay.
The numbers of NG tests performed, and NG diagnoses reported in 2025 by the two SHSs were extracted from the GUMCAD STI Surveillance System (10).
The upper and lower 95% confidence interval limits were used to estimate a plausible range of missed infections.
This study was undertaken for health protection purposes.
This study did not involve human participants.
All clinical samples tested were residual, anonymised, and unlinked from any identifiable information prior to testing.
In total 978 Xpert® NG-negative clinical specimens (179 vaginal swabs, 397 rectal swabs and 402 urine specimens) were tested on the GeneProof TM Neisseria gonorrhoeae PCR kit.
The majority of which (975/978, 99.7%) were confirmed as NG-negative or returned an NG-indeterminate result on the alternate assay (Table 1).
text.formatted: The majority of which (975/978, 99.7%) were confirmed as NG-negative or returned an NG-indeterminate result on the alternate assay (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Three specimens (3/978, 0.3%), two rectal swabs and one urine sample, from three individuals (inferred from patient age) from the same clinic, tested positive on the GeneProof TM assay (Table 1).
text.formatted: Three specimens (3/978, 0.3%), two rectal swabs and one urine sample, from three individuals (inferred from patient age) from the same clinic, tested positive on the GeneProof TM assay (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Xpert® CT/NG assay re-testing Sufficient residual volume remained for two of the NG-positive samples (both rectal) to allow re-testing on the Xpert® CT/NG assay.
Both samples retested NG-negative (Table 1).
text.formatted: Both samples retested NG-negative (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Review of the individual target amplification reports revealed that either NG2 or NG4 was amplified (Table 1), but not both, which is required for a positive Xpert® result.
text.formatted: Review of the individual target amplification reports revealed that either NG2 or NG4 was amplified (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>), but not both, which is required for a positive Xpert® result.

text.text: Therefore at least 2/978 (0.2%) of the specimens analysed were confirmed as false-negative results on the Xpert® CT/NG assay, and had result profiles consistent with previously detected diagnostic escape mutants (8, 9).
text.formatted: Therefore at least 2/978 (0.2%) of the specimens analysed were confirmed as false-negative results on the Xpert® CT/NG assay, and had result profiles consistent with previously detected diagnostic escape mutants <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9)</ref>.

text.text: The remaining specimen that was insufficient for re-testing was classified as a "suspected" mutant.
In 2025, the two sexual health clinics participating in this study performed 62,404 NG tests, of which 7,396 (11.9%) were reported as NG-positive (10).

Using the lower and upper 95% confidence limits reported in Table 1, it was estimated that between 62 and 562 tests were falsely reported as NG-negative due to the presence of an escape mutant in 2025.
text.formatted: Using the lower and upper 95% confidence limits reported in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>, it was estimated that between 62 and 562 tests were falsely reported as NG-negative due to the presence of an escape mutant in 2025.

text.text: This prospective case-finding study investigated NG diagnostic escape mutants for the Xpert® CT/NG assay in two large SHSs using the assay in clinic as a nearpatient diagnostic test.

Re-testing of NG-negative specimens with an alternate assay at the national STI Reference Laboratory confirmed the original NG-negative result for 99.7% of specimens (including specimens categorised as NG-indeterminate).
However, two (0.2%) single-target Xpert® NG mutants containing specimens were detected.
A further specimen was classified as a possible mutant.
All confirmed and possible NG-mutants were sourced from different patients attending the same clinic (Clinic 1).
In this analysis, NG-indeterminate specimens were grouped with the NGnegative samples as evidence of NG-specific DNA could not be reliably detected in these specimens using the GeneProof TM assay.
This may be due to differences in the analytical sensitivity of the tests or cross-reactivity of the GeneProof TM assay as well as false-negative results on the Xpert® NG assay.

The requirement for both NG assay targets (NG2 and NG4) to detect amplification to return a positive result is assumed to enhance specificity and prevent over-reporting where amplification in one target is due to cross-reactivity with other Neisseria species, a well-known problem in NG diagnostics.
However, this cautious approach results in vulnerability to under-reporting of true NG diagnoses, where a single-target mutant is present, such as those detected in this study.
The GeneProof TM assay contains two NG-specific targets that are different to the targets within the Xpert® NG assay.
However, both report in the same channel therefore it is not possible to discern whether one or both targets have amplified.
For the two confirmed mutant specimens, on review of the individual Xpert® sample reports, a positive signal was recorded for either the NG2 or NG4 target.
Therefore, the samples were positive for at least two independent NG-specific targets, indicating that the NG-positive results were genuine, and not a result of cross-reactivity.

Although this study was not designed to determine the prevalence of Xpert® CT/NG escape mutants, our findings suggest that some under-reporting of gonorrhoea diagnoses may occur in clinics using the Xpert® CT/NG assay.
Reassuringly, the vast majority of samples were confirmed as NG-negative.
Further studies involving a broader and more geographically diverse range of clinics are required to better understand the prevalence and distribution of these mutants.
The samples included in this study were anonymised prior to testing.

Whilst this was a pragmatic approach as testing was not performed in real-time, it did limit the interpretation of the findings as it was not possible to review the patient records to understand if NG had been diagnosed through other means, and assess the potential impact of the false-negative report.
Symptomatic patients would be subject to clinical follow-up including repeat testing.
Therefore, it is likely that infections within this group would be captured in real-time and treated appropriately.

A further limitation of this study was exclusion of Chlamydia trachomatis-positive, NG-negative rectal swabs which were unavailable due to referral to a separate laboratory for detection of Lymphogranuloma venereum genovars (as per current national guidance (11)).
text.formatted: A further limitation of this study was exclusion of Chlamydia trachomatis-positive, NG-negative rectal swabs which were unavailable due to referral to a separate laboratory for detection of Lymphogranuloma venereum genovars (as per current national guidance <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(11)</ref>).

text.text: Future studies should incorporate these important samples so as not to restrict prevalence estimates.
Finally, this study utilised residual clinical specimens, which whilst convenient, prevented further characterisation of the mutants detected due to lack of sample volume for additional testing.
Future studies could consider testing cultured isolates in place of clinical specimens to enable genome sequencing and other downstream characterisation of putative escape mutants.
Overall, the study demonstrates the high sensitivity of the Xpert® CT/NG assay.

A small number of diagnostic escape mutants were detected and extrapolations from this indicate that there may be some missed gonorrhoea diagnoses from providers using this assay as a primary diagnostic test.
Further work is required to comprehensively investigate the true prevalence of these mutants, and any clinical impact of under-reporting.
